title: Ponavljanje
theme: Review of Lessons 1 to 6, plus postcards from across BiH
reviewerNotes: Copy cleaned (no em dashes, no Week title). Civic section added. Ready for human review.
storyBeat: Ana captions what she learned in Lessons 1 to 6. Emir then slides in postcards from Jajce, Blagaj, and Počitelj so the review opens more of the country.

vocabulary: Recycle Lessons 1 to 6: greetings, biti, numbers and café, family, places, time
Light diary words: sedmica, foto, priča
grammar: Remember sam, si, je and moj, moja
Remember Gdje je…? and Koliko je sati?
culture: Photo captions as a memory tool
New places beyond the usual tourist pair: Jajce, Blagaj on the Buna, and Počitelj

grammar.title: Remember. biti and possessives
grammar.explanation: Core so far: Ja sam Ana. Ti si Emir. On je / Ona je… Pair with possessives: Moj prijatelj. Moja prijateljica. Moja mačka. If a noun ends in -a, try moja first.

examples.bosnian: Ja sam Ana. Ti si Emir.
examples.english: I am Ana. You are Emir.

grammar.title: Remember. where and when
grammar.explanation: Place kit: Gdje je…? Ovdje. Tamo. U Sarajevu. Kod Amire. Time kit: Koliko je sati? Danas / sutra + weekday. Put them in one diary line: Danas sam kod Amire. Sutra. mapa!

examples.bosnian: Koliko je sati? Deset je sati.
examples.english: What time is it? It is ten.

culture.title: A diary, then postcards from farther out
culture.body: Ana can caption Sebilj and kahva now. Emir refuses to let the review shrink Bosnia and Herzegovina to two postcard cities. He adds three images from across the country: the Pliva waterfall at Jajce, where a river falls through the town; the Blagaj tekija under a cliff at the Buna spring; and Počitelj’s stone houses stacked above the Neretva valley. Review the language first. Then aim your next sutra at a wider map. The café is home base. The classroom is the whole country.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson A: Recycle the toolkit
lessonBlocks.body: Rapid fire without notes: Zdravo! Ja sam… Drago mi je. Kahvu, molim. Koliko? Moj brat. Moja sestra. Gdje je mapa? Ovdje. Tamo. Koliko je sati? Danas. Sutra. Emir times Ana for two minutes. Misses are fine. Laugh, repeat, and move on. Circle three weak words and write them once with the correct letters.
tips: Speed first, then one careful rewrite
Revisit č ć š ž đ from Lesson 1 if your spelling slips

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson B: Photo diary captions
lessonBlocks.body: Caption six lines for skills from Lessons 1 to 6. Then add three place lines Emir teaches as teases: Jajce, vodopad. Blagaj, Buna. Počitelj, stari grad. Glue them with Gdje je…? and Tamo. Share the diary at the table. Amira closes the lesson with Hvala, and sutra! Lesson 8 will bring burek and more of the map.
tips: Lines from Lessons 1 to 6 come first, then three new place names
Reuse Gdje je…? and Tamo for the postcard stack

funFacts.title: Jajce, town on a waterfall
funFacts.body: In Jajce the Pliva River drops as a waterfall right by the old town. It is a rare urban cascade and a medieval royal seat of the Bosnian kingdom.

funFacts.title: Blagaj and the Buna spring
funFacts.body: At Blagaj, a Dervish tekija sits under a cliff where the Buna River bursts from the rock. It is one of the strongest karst springs in the region.

funFacts.title: Počitelj’s stone stack
funFacts.body: Počitelj climbs a hillside in Herzegovina in stone houses and a fortress silhouette. It is a preserved Ottoman-era settlement above the Neretva corridor.

funFacts.title: Banja Luka on the mental map
funFacts.body: Farther north, Banja Luka spreads along the Vrbas with the Kastel fortress. Reviews should keep adding real towns so BiH never shrinks to two postcard cities.

civicContext.title: A state built so one entity can block the rest
civicContext.body: Dayton divided Bosnia and Herzegovina into two entities, the Federation of BiH and Republika Srpska, and many state decisions require agreement across that structure. The design stopped the war, but it also lets obstruction at entity level delay reforms that EU accession demands. This review lesson is a good place to say it plainly: language practice can move every day, while the constitutional machine can still freeze the country in place.
